claims.text: There are three common reasons a reader pays for what they read, because they have to, because they feel they have to, and because it is the right thing to do, and most reader-funded publishing uses one of them.
claims.quote: There are three common reasons a reader pays for what they read, and most reader-funded publishing uses one of them.

claims.text: The Guardian's app sits within a paywall in which free users can only read 20 articles a month, Press Gazette reported in September 2025.
claims.quote: sits within a paywall (free users can only read 20 articles per month)

claims.text: The Guardian's middle tier, at £12 a month, buys among other things the right to avoid intrusive pop-up supporter messages: the feeling of being asked has a price.
claims.quote: avoid intrusive pop-up supporter messages

claims.text: The Wikimedia Foundation reports over 8 million donors giving an average donation of $10.58 in its 2023-24 financial year, reached by asking everybody every year.
claims.quote: over 8 million donors giving an average donation of $10.58

claims.text: All three reasons work to a degree, but they do not scale for anyone who is not already enormous, and they make the reader feel the wrong thing.
claims.quote: they do not scale for anyone who is not already enormous, and that they make the reader feel the wrong thing

claims.text: The reader should pay because paying helps them, not out of guilt, shame or moral obligation.
claims.quote: The reader should pay because paying helps them.

claims.text: What a reader is buying is not the article, which is free, but time, context, focus, the ability to make good decisions, a streamlined way through and a better experience.
claims.quote: The article is free to read here, and it is free to read with the meter below zero.

claims.text: Each of those depends on a record of what the reader read, how much, what they kept and rejected; the reading meter already keeps that record because a ledger has to.
claims.quote: The reading meter already keeps that record, because a ledger has to.

claims.text: Reading builds a persona weighted by how far down each page the reader went, named from the topics read most until the reader names it, with a front page and a graph.
claims.quote: It gets a name from the topics you read most, until you give it one of your own

claims.text: Every pick has Keep and Not for this persona, and every article has Keep in your persona; the reader can see the model the site has of them and change it.
claims.quote: the reader can see the model the site has of them, and change it

claims.text: The second lesson from building The Cyber Boardroom is that once users try personalisation they do not want one persona, they want several.
claims.quote: once users try personalisation, they do not want one persona, they want several

claims.text: A persona is a way to manage focus: one for security, one for AI development, one for everything else, and the more a reader can do with it the more attached they become.
claims.quote: A persona is a way to manage focus.

claims.text: Five ready-made personas, the founder, the journalist, the security lead, the AI builder and the board member, each start from seven or eight articles and a few topics.
claims.quote: Each one starts from seven or eight articles and a few topics, and becomes yours as you read and curate.

claims.text: Today a persona lives in one browser; opening the site on an iPad and then a laptop makes two strangers, which is not a security gap but a bad user experience that gets worse as the product gets better.
claims.quote: Two devices, two strangers, is not a security gap; it is a bad user experience

claims.text: The first meter article called a fresh private window a cheat; the reader who does it was not going to pay anyway.
claims.quote: the reader who does it was not going to pay anyway

claims.text: The only fix today is manual and clumsy on purpose: export the account as JSON on one device and restore it on the other.
claims.quote: export your account as JSON on one device and restore it on the other

claims.text: What people will pay for is a persona that follows them to their phone, their laptop and their agent, so that connecting through Claude reads as their security persona and not as a stranger.
claims.quote: They pay because they want to keep their persona, and to have it wherever they read.

claims.text: When the persona moves off the browser it moves into an encrypted vault whose key only the reader holds, so the site that stores it cannot read it and the reader can take it elsewhere.
claims.quote: it moves into an encrypted vault whose key only the reader holds, so the site that stores it cannot read it

claims.text: There are about sixty articles on the site today across six topics, chosen so each starting persona has a real shelf; the better each article's graph, the better every persona built on it.
claims.quote: There are about sixty articles on this site today, across six topics

claims.text: Readers can send their reading, which pages, how far, what they kept, and get back a front page designed from it: the tightest feedback loop available.
claims.quote: It is the tightest feedback loop we have: real reading in, a real front page back.

claims.text: H6: when a persona can follow a reader between devices for a price, more readers pay for that than top up the meter for reading alone.
claims.quote: more readers pay for that than top up the meter for reading alone

claims.text: H7: readers who have more than one persona pay more often than readers who have one.
claims.quote: Readers who have more than one persona pay more often than readers who have one

claims.text: H6 and H7 cannot be tested until a persona can follow a reader between devices; they are written down so nobody can pretend later to have expected something else.
claims.quote: They cannot be tested until a persona can follow a reader between devices

claims.text: Personas are in SG Meter v1.1; the five starting personas are defined in the build, which refuses one that names an article that does not exist.
claims.quote: the build refuses one that names an article that does not exist
